comparisons.peer_topic: Total Liabilities and Drivers of Change
comparisons.peer_summary: At December 31, 2024, total liabilities were approximately $3.0 trillion, an increase of $77.5 billion from December 31, 2023, driven by higher federal funds purchased, securities loaned or sold under agreements to repurchase, deposits, and short-term borrowings, partially offset by lower long-term debt.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC report on the total liabilities of their consolidated balance sheets and identify the primary drivers of year-over-year increases. GS reported total liabilities of $1.55 trillion, an increase of $29.29 billion, driven by collateralized financings and deposits. BAC reported total liabilities of approximately $3.0 trillion, an increase of $77.5 billion, driven by federal funds purchased, securities loaned/repurchase agreements, deposits, and short-term borrowings. While both cite deposits as a growth driver, GS highlights collateralized financings, whereas BAC highlights wholesale funding instruments like federal funds and repos.

sentences.text: As of December 2024, total liabilities in our consolidated balance sheets were $1.55 trillion, an increase of $29.29 billion from December 2023, primarily reflecting increases in collateralized financings of $35.03 billion (reflecting the impact of our and our clients' activities), and deposits of $4.60 billion (due to an increase in consumer deposits, partially offset by decreases in transaction banking deposits and other deposits), partially offset by decreases in customer and other payables of $7.47 billion (primarily reflecting our clients' activities) and borrowings of $5.48 billion (driven by net maturities).

At December 31, 2024, total liabilities were approximately $3.0 trillion, up $77.5 billion from December 31, 2023, primarily due to higher federal funds purchased and securities loaned or sold under agreements to repurchase, deposits, and short-term borrowings, partially offset by lower long-term debt.

Both firms detail segment-specific or product-specific drivers within their deposit liabilities.

• an increase in CIB due to net inflows predominantly in Payments, largely offset by net maturities of structured notes in Markets,

• an increase in AWM as a result of growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, reflecting the impact of higher-yielding product offerings, largely offset by continued migration into other investments, and

• a decline in CCB primarily driven by a decrease in balances in existing accounts due to increased customer spending and migration into higher-yielding investments, predominantly offset by new accounts.
